transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 14:30 PST
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Clara Nguyen (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (CTO, CobaltSight), Jonah Reed (Lead ML Eng), Priya Singh (Infra)

Summary:
Quick discovery to size hosted vs dedicated vs private for their customer-facing assistant. Primary focus: p95 latency targets, concurrency, streaming performance and token/sec throughput for bursty traffic. Customer is sensitive to data residency and KMS controls.

Topics:
- Current stack and production RPS/latency
- p95 targets and SLOs
- Streaming vs non-streaming use cases
- Benchmarking approach (synthetic vs replay)
- Security and private deployment constraints
- Next steps and responsibilities

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining. is this time still good?
[00:03] Maya: yeah yep sorry, got pulled into a standup but i'm here.
[00:06] Samir: great. i'm samir patel from Redwood, AE. with me is clara, our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Clara: hi all, happy to dig in, especially on streaming and p95 behavior.
[00:16] Maya: awesome, i'll hand it off to jonah to give quick context on where we're at.
[00:19] Jonah: cool. so CobaltSight runs an assistant for our docs+support workflows. average peak concurrent users is about 1200, but bursts up to ~3k during promos. average prompt length is 120 tokens, some are long threads up to 1.5k tokens. our current self-hosted setup uses mixed A100 and some 8-bit quantized models in prod. p95 under current infra is about 380 ms for short queries but for longer context threads it jumps to 1.2s which users notice.
[00:45] Priya: to add, we have strict residency requirements for EMEA customers and want KMS integration for key rotation - HSM is a plus. So private deployment is on the table.
[00:53] Samir: thanks, that's super helpful. couple quick clarifying q's — when you say bursts to 3k, is that sustained for minutes or seconds? and are the 1.5k token threads frequent?
[01:02] Jonah: bursts are typically 30-90 seconds, but can repeat several times a day. long threads are maybe 2-3% of hits but they drive most of the cost and latency.
[01:10] Clara: got it. what are your p95 targets? do you have an SLO?
[01:14] Maya: for the product team we want p95 < 500ms for standard conversational queries and p95 < 1.5s for long threads. If we can get the standard ones to sub-300 that'd be ideal, but cost tradeoffs matter.
[01:26] Samir: makes sense. so three levers we'll discuss: model selection/quantization, dedicated vs hosted routing, and batching/cache. also streaming - are you using streaming tokens to render progressively in the UI?
[01:36] Jonah: yes, streaming for long answers is used. we also do partial renders for code completions so low latency per initial token is important.
[01:44] Clara: okay. i'll call out real quick how Redwood approaches this: for hosted we recommend a curated model variant with token-level streaming optimized kernels; for Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools which helps for tail latencies during bursts; for Private we can bring the same runtime but with a private control plane + KMS integration.
[02:02] Maya: one concern — cost. Dedicated sounds great for tail but we need to justify the monthly commit. any heuristics on break-even for a workload like ours?
[02:09] Samir: yes, we'll run a cost model against your traffic trace, but quick rule: if you have sustained high concurrency (hundreds to thousands) and predictable bursts, Dedicated often beats hosted on unit cost and gives p95 predictability. for sporadic bursts, hosted with autoscale and burst pools can be cheaper. we'll quantify.
[02:28] Jonah: on benchmarking — we can share anonymized traces. we want to test token/sec throughput and p95 under 1) steady load at 800 qps, 2) burst profile 0->3k in 30s, 3) mixed with 3% long threads. how do you typically run that?
[02:41] Clara: ideal is replay of your traces in our harness (we run a synthetic driver that respects inter-arrival and token length distribution). also we'll include a streaming-specific test that checks initial token latency and sustained token/sec. for p95 we sample across steady and burst windows.
[02:55] Samir: we'll propose three traffic profiles and target metrics: p95 standard <500ms (goal 300ms), p95 long threads <1.5s, sustained token/sec target per-node (we'll propose 500-1,200 tokens/sec depending on quant and model), and end-to-end streaming latency for first token sub-150ms if possible.
[03:18] Maya: those per-node numbers — do you mean per GPU instance? what's the variability across model quant configs? we use a custom LLaMA-derivative.
[03:26] Clara: yes per serving worker / GPU. quantization to int8 or q4_0 gives big throughput improvements but sometimes degrades some outputs; we recommend running quality-evals in the loop. kernel selection in our runtime also affects token/sec — some architectures do much better for long sequences. we'll map recommendations to your model.
[03:45] Jonah: and what's the story on KV cache / long context — do you partition cache across pods or keep it warm?
[03:51] Clara: Redwood has automatic KV cache sharding and prefix caching for repeated contexts; for private deployments you can configure sticky routing to keep KV hot, or we use a shared cache in Dedicated pools to reduce recompute. there are tradeoffs with memory footprint vs warm hit rate.
[04:08] Priya: for security we need SSO/SCIM, RBAC, audit logs, and at-rest encryption with customer-managed keys. also, can we keep logs for 90 days and accessible to our SIEM?
[04:19] Samir: yes — SAML/SSO, SCIM, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logs are standard for Enterprise. for Private you can opt to store logs in your VPC and plug into your SIEM. KMS/HSM integration is supported; we'll share the whitepaper.
[04:34] Maya: great. another question — fallback behavior during capacity shortages, we can't have the assistant go offline. can Redwood auto-fallback to a smaller model or degrade gracefully?
[04:44] Clara: yes, smart routing and fallbacks are built-in: policy-driven fallback to cheaper model variants, weighted routing across regions, and graceful degrade with partial responses. you can set hard SLOs to trigger canary fallback.
[04:56] Jonah: nice. about streaming — when we render tokens incrementally, sometimes the first chunk is delayed more than the rest. what's the main cause and how do you mitigate?
[05:04] Clara: often it's the initial decode + model KV warmup. we mitigate with prefix caching, warm pools for streaming sessions, and prioritized short-path kernels for the first tokens. also batching strategies can be tuned so that initial tokens get lower batching latency.
[05:20] Maya: on the implementation side, if we go private on-prem, do you bring a control plane or is it fully customer-managed?
[05:26] Samir: we offer a private control plane option where orchestration stays with Redwood but networking and data never leave your VPC. fully air-gapped on-prem packages are also possible for regulated environments; Clara can share the checklist.
[05:38] Priya: bandwidth — our on-prem cluster is connected but we want to avoid egress. will model weights stay local?
[05:45] Clara: yes, for Private and on-prem the model artifacts and weights reside in your environment. we can coordinate updates; nothing has to leave your VPC unless you opt in.
[05:54] Jonah: on benchmarking tooling, how do you measure p95 across streaming vs non-streaming? do you stitch client-side render times or server-side timings?
[06:02] Clara: we do both. server-side gives pure inference latency; client-side captures RTT and render time. we recommend instrumenting both so you can break down contribution from network, tokenization, and server decode. our console shows token-level timing and per-route SLOs.
[06:18] Samir: okay to talk about next steps — we will need your traffic trace, sample prompts, and a list of critical flows. we'll propose a benchmark plan with three profiles and include cost estimates for hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[06:30] Maya: yes, we'll compile that. one ask — can you include a conservative estimate for on-prem capacity sizing (number of GPUs) for the burst profile?
[06:36] Samir: absolutely. we'll size both steady-state and burst headroom. for a rough back-of-envelope, given your 3k 30s bursts and token lengths, you might need X nodes with 8k token/sec aggregate; we'll confirm with the trace.
[06:50] Jonah: can we also do a quick token-level quality baseline? i'm worried quantization might change hallucination rates for some prompts.
[06:56] Clara: yes, we'll run a quality/regression eval on a sample prompt set and include pass/fail thresholds. we can also do A/B with quant variants.
[07:05] Maya: timeline — we're aiming to decide by mid-Jan for Q1 rollout. does that align with Redwood's pilot calendar?
[07:12] Samir: yes, if we kick off benchmarks in mid-Dec and complete them by early Jan, we can do a pilot in late Jan. seems doable.
[07:18] Priya: final infra note — we use Okta for SSO, and our procurement needs SOC2 + DPAs.
[07:24] Samir: we'll include SOC2 cert and standard DPA.
[07:27] Clara: i'll add the KMS/HSM integration notes and a runnable checklist for private deploy.
[07:31] Maya: thanks, appreciate it.
[07:33] Samir: quick recap of action items and who owns what?
[07:36] Samir: Samir will draft benchmark plan with three traffic profiles and p95/token/sec targets; Clara will share private deployment + KMS checklist and SOC2 whitepaper; Maya/Jonah will provide anonymized traces and sample prompts. target dates in the follow-up.
[07:52] Maya: sounds good.
[07:54] Samir: any other Qs?
[07:55] Jonah: none from me.
[07:56] Priya: not now.
[07:57] Samir: great, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and a calendar invite for a kickoff in mid-Dec. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
